lead: A hydrodynamic journal bearing carries a rotating shaft on a film of oil. The shaft turns inside a slightly larger sleeve. It drags oil into a gap that narrows in the direction of rotation. Viscous drag pushes oil through that wedge, pressure rises, and the pressure balances the load. Metal surfaces stay apart while the shaft runs. You meet these bearings in steam turbines, pumps, motors, gearboxes and crankshafts. The design question is simple to state: can the oil film stay thick enough at the running speed, load and viscosity?
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for viscosity and Chapter 5.2 for sliding contact.

blocks.text: A hydrodynamic journal bearing is a plain sleeve around a shaft. The journal diameter D and bearing length L set the size; both are in mm. The journal radius is r = D/2. The radial clearance c is the small difference between the bearing radius and the journal radius. It is often a small fraction of a millimetre. Diametral clearance is twice the radial clearance; do not use it as c.
The shaft centre sits off the bearing centre by the eccentricity e. The eccentricity ratio is ε = e/c, a pure number. The closest gap is the minimum film thickness h₀.
ε = e / c,   h₀ = c − e = c(1 − ε)
blocks.where: e is the journal centre shift from the bearing centre, c is the radial clearance, ε is the eccentricity ratio, and h₀ is the minimum film thickness; e, c and h₀ use the same length unit.

blocks.text: When the shaft turns, oil sticking to the journal is dragged into the clearance. The gap narrows in the direction of rotation, so the oil flow must pass a smaller area. Pressure rises in this wedge. The pressure peak lies between the start of the wedge and the minimum film; the resultant pressure balances the external load. The journal centre moves until this balance is reached. The angle between the load line and the line joining the centres is the attitude angle. Reynolds equation gives the film pressure; here we use its results and do not derive it. Some syllabi call these fluid-film bearings.

Three lubrication regimes matter. In boundary lubrication the oil film is too thin; high spots touch and carry load, so wear occurs. In mixed lubrication the film carries part of the load and high spots carry part. In hydrodynamic lubrication a full film separates the surfaces, and pressure in the oil carries the whole load. This chapter is about the third regime.

The pressure distribution is not uniform. Positive pressure builds in the converging half of the clearance. In the diverging half the pressure falls toward ambient and the oil may cavitate (form vapour pockets). Cavities cannot carry tensile load, so the positive region does the useful work. Oil grooves supply oil to the bearing. Put feed grooves in a low-pressure or unloaded region. A circumferential groove running across the loaded film lets pressure escape and lowers load capacity. Supply must be continuous; starvation collapses the film.

Starts and stops cause the most wear. At zero speed there is no hydrodynamic film, so the surfaces run in boundary or mixed contact. Large machines start the oil pump before the shaft and stop the shaft before the pump. Frequent starts shorten bearing life. Hydrodynamic action needs enough speed, enough viscosity and enough oil; when any one falls, the film thins.

A design must keep h₀ above the combined surface roughness, any expected debris and a safety margin. h₀ depends on c, ε, viscosity, speed, load, L/D and temperature. A smaller c raises load capacity but lowers oil flow and raises temperature. A larger c raises oil flow and cooling, but h₀ rises with c only up to an optimum; beyond it the journal runs more eccentric and the film thins again. A long bearing (large L/D) carries more load but is sensitive to misalignment; a short bearing leaks oil from its ends.

Viscosity must be taken at the operating temperature. Hot oil is thinner, so a bearing that is safe when cold may fail when hot. Friction power becomes heat, and that heat lowers viscosity. Design is therefore iterative: choose c, L/D and oil grade, estimate ε and h₀, then check temperature and oil flow. The Sommerfeld number (Chapter 5.4) groups speed, viscosity, load and clearance; the Raimondi and Boyd charts (Chapter 5.5) give ε, h₀, friction and flow.

sections.h3: Petroff's equation and the friction curve

blocks.text: A lightly loaded or very fast journal hardly moves off centre, so the film is close to a uniform ring of thickness c. The oil is then sheared like the film between two plates: velocity U = 2πrn at the journal, zero at the bush. Shear stress τ = μU/c acts on the whole journal surface 2πrL, and the friction torque is that force times r.
T = 4π² μ n r³ L / c,   f = 2π² (μn/p)(r/c)
blocks.where: T is the friction torque in N·m; μ in Pa·s; n in rev/s; r, L and c in m; p = W/(2rL) is the bearing pressure in Pa; f = T/(W r) is the friction coefficient. This is Petroff's equation. It ignores eccentricity, so it underestimates friction in a heavily loaded bearing.

blocks.text: Plot f against the bearing modulus μN/p (N in rpm) and you get the friction curve. At small μN/p the film is thin and friction is high (boundary and mixed); friction falls to a minimum, then rises in a straight line once the film is full, as Petroff predicts. A common textbook rule keeps the working μN/p about three times the value at the minimum, so a dip in speed or a hot spell does not push the bearing back into mixed lubrication.

spec.aria: A journal off centre in its bush, with eccentricity 0.03 millimetres, minimum film 0.02 millimetres opposite the widest gap of 0.08 millimetres, the load W and the rotation.

examples.question: A journal bearing has journal diameter D = 50 mm, radial clearance c = 0.05 mm and eccentricity ratio ε = 0.6. Find the eccentricity e and the minimum film thickness h₀. Give h₀ in mm and in μm.
steps: Data: D = 50 mm (not needed for e and h₀), c = 0.05 mm, ε = 0.6.
From ε = e/c, e = ε c = 0.6 × 0.05 mm = 0.03 mm.
examples.answer: e = 0.03 mm and h₀ = 0.02 mm = 20 μm.

examples.question: A lightly loaded fan bearing has journal diameter 60 mm, length 60 mm and radial clearance 0.06 mm. It carries 1.8 kN at 3000 rpm with oil of μ = 0.015 Pa·s. Use Petroff's equation to find the friction coefficient, the friction torque and the power lost.
steps: Bearing pressure: p = W/(2rL) = 1800/(0.06 × 0.06) = 5.0 × 10⁵ Pa = 0.5 MPa.
Is Petroff fair here? S = (μn/p)(r/c)² = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 250 000 = 0.375, a light load with the journal near centre, so yes.
examples.answer: f = 0.0148, T = 0.799 N·m and the friction power is about 251 W.

traps: Radial versus diametral clearance: if a drawing gives 0.10 mm on diameter, c = 0.05 mm. Use c in h₀ = c(1 − ε).
h₀ is the smallest gap, not the centre shift e. With c = 0.05 mm and ε = 0.6, e = 0.03 mm but h₀ = 0.02 mm.
Using Petroff's equation for a heavily loaded bearing. It assumes a centred journal and gives too little friction once ε is large.
An oil-filled bearing at rest is not hydrodynamic. It runs in boundary or mixed contact until speed builds.
A groove in the loaded film lowers load capacity; feed oil to the unloaded or low-pressure side.

quiz.q: Define eccentricity ratio ε in a journal bearing.
quiz.a: ε = e/c, where e is the journal centre shift from the bearing centre and c is the radial clearance; ε is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does pressure build in the converging gap of a journal bearing?
quiz.a: The turning journal drags oil into a gap that narrows. The oil must pass a smaller area, and viscous resistance raises the pressure. This pressure supports the load.

quiz.q: A bearing has radial clearance c = 0.06 mm and eccentricity ratio ε = 0.5. Find e and h₀.
Oil temperature rises and viscosity falls. Load and speed are unchanged. What happens to ε and h₀?
quiz.a: Lower viscosity gives a weaker film pressure at the same speed, so the journal centre moves further from the bearing centre, towards the bush wall on the loaded side. ε increases and h₀ decreases.

quiz.q: Name the three lubrication regimes of a sliding bearing.
quiz.a: Boundary lubrication, mixed lubrication and hydrodynamic lubrication.

quiz.q: Why is a circumferential oil groove in the loaded region bad for load capacity?
quiz.a: It connects high-pressure oil to low-pressure oil, so pressure leaks away. The film pressure that carries the load falls.

quiz.q: Why does a motor bearing wear mainly during start and stop, not at full speed?
quiz.a: At low speed the hydrodynamic film is not built, so boundary or mixed contact occurs. At full speed the oil film separates the surfaces.

quiz.q: Using Petroff's equation, find f for μ = 0.02 Pa·s, n = 25 rev/s, p = 1 MPa and r/c = 500.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial turbines often use tilting-pad journal bearings: several pads can tilt and form their own oil wedges, which improves stability at high speed. Researchers solve the Reynolds equation numerically with temperature and turbulence effects, and monitor oil pressure, temperature and vibration to catch film failure early. Search terms: tilting-pad bearing, thermohydrodynamic lubrication, bearing cavitation.
